{"translation_en":"ROXANE:\nOh! He cannot go on importuning me forever!\n(Unsealing the letter):\n**I love you**, and if...\n(By the light of Ragueneau’s lantern, she moves aside and reads in a low voice):\nMademoiselle,\nThe drums\nAre beating; my regiment is fastening its doublets.\nIt is leaving; they think I have already gone—but I remain.\nI disobey you. I am in this convent.\nI am coming to you, and am informing you beforehand\nThrough a friar as simple as a goat,\nWho can understand nothing of this. Your lips\nSmiled too much upon me earlier: I wished to see them again.\nSend everyone away, and deign to receive\nThe audacious man already pardoned, I hope,\nWho signs himself your most... et cetera...\n(To the Capuchin):\nFather,\nHere is what this letter tells me. Listen:\n(Everyone draws closer; she reads aloud):\nMademoiselle,\nYou must submit to the wishes\nOf the Cardinal, however hard that may be for you.\nThat is why I have chosen, to place\nThese lines in your charming hands, a most holy,\nMost intelligent and discreet Capuchin;\nWe wish him to give you, and in your—","larger_context_summary":"In Act III, Roxane receives this letter from the Comte de Guiche, her powerful and unwelcome suitor, while Christian and Cyrano are nearby. De Guiche’s regiment is departing for war, but he has secretly remained behind to visit her and has entrusted the message to an unsuspecting Capuchin. Roxane privately reads his amorous declaration and plan, then immediately exploits the messenger’s ignorance: aloud, she fabricates a different letter in which the Cardinal supposedly commands the friar to marry her to Christian. The stakes therefore extend beyond courtship. Roxane is trying to secure her desired marriage, evade De Guiche’s advances, and manipulate ecclesiastical and aristocratic authority before the military departure changes everyone’s circumstances.","interpretive_commentary":"The highlighted clause is a compact written avowal whose primary force is to present the writer’s love for Roxane as true. Although De Guiche’s sincerity may be doubted—and his pursuit is intrusive—that possible deception does not alter the clause’s truth-conditional form. Nor does the declaration itself perform a marriage, promise fidelity, or otherwise institute a new relationship; any practical consequences arise from the surrounding courtship and Roxane’s response. Its emotional subject matter is intense, but the wording is composed correspondence rather than an involuntary or reflexive outburst, which explains the absence of expressive force in the narrower sense. The occurrence is also valuable as a revoiced case: Roxane briefly voices De Guiche’s written words without adopting them as her own. Her subsequent fraudulent public “reading” deceives the Capuchin, but that later manipulation belongs to the dramatic framing, not to the semantics of “I love you.”"}
